questions.question: What does the Chinchilla scaling law suggest about the relationship between model size and training data?
choices: Bigger models always perform better regardless of data size
For a given compute budget, there is an optimal ratio of model parameters to training tokens — both should scale together
Training data size is irrelevant once the model exceeds 1 billion parameters
Smaller models with more data always outperform larger models
questions.explanation: Chinchilla's key insight is compute-optimal scaling: given a fixed compute budget, you should balance model size and dataset size proportionally rather than over-parameterizing a model with insufficient data.

questions.question: What is the practical significance of the compute-optimal ratio in scaling laws?
choices: It tells you exactly how many GPUs to buy
It helps estimate whether investing compute in a larger model or more training data will yield better performance per dollar
It guarantees that the model will achieve human-level performance
It only applies to models with fewer than 1 billion parameters
questions.explanation: The compute-optimal ratio guides resource allocation — if your model is over-parameterized relative to its data, you'd get better returns by either collecting more data or using a smaller model at the same compute cost.

questions.question: What happens when a model is significantly over-parameterized (too many parameters relative to training data)?
choices: The model becomes more robust to all types of inputs
The model tends to memorize training data rather than learning generalizable patterns, leading to overfitting
The model automatically adjusts its own parameter count
questions.explanation: Over-parameterized models with insufficient data tend to memorize rather than generalize. Scaling laws help identify the sweet spot where model capacity matches data availability for optimal generalization.
